definition: Ruse means a trick aimed at misleading a particular target for a specific purpose.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ruse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ruse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her 'forgotten' scarf was a ruse — an excuse to knock a second time and count who was sitting at the table now.
Trick is milder than ruse — any small deception or prank counts as a trick, planned or not.
Hoax goes further than ruse: a ruse misleads a chosen target toward a goal, while a hoax sets out to fool a whole public.

A ploy is a calculated maneuver toward a tactical goal — sneaky, but not always a deception at all: a delaying ploy can be perfectly open about what it is. A ruse is always a deception and always aimed, built to move a particular target into a particular mistake.

A stratagem is a scheme with a battlefield flavor, grander and more elaborate than a ruse, and deployed against an opponent in some contest. A ruse can be as small as a 'forgotten' scarf; a stratagem implies a campaign. Both deceive, but a stratagem needs an adversary.

French ruser produced ruse and then stopped: no prefix, no suffix, no English cousins. (Rush and Russia only rhyme with it by accident.) The word survives alone because hunters, soldiers, and detectives kept finding it useful.
Ruse means a trick aimed at misleading a particular target for a specific purpose.
The recall notice was a ruse: collectors who brought their counterfeit coins in for a 'safety exchange' were met at the counter by two detectives.
A ruse is one engineered deception with a job to do.
A trick can be as small as a prank, and a hoax fools a whole public just to see if it can — a ruse is aimed, built to move a particular person into a particular mistake.
Ruse is short, slightly Frenchified, and precise: one engineered deception with a target and a purpose.
Prefer trick for anything casual, hoax when the public itself is the mark, and legerdemain — this unit's other French import — when what impresses you is the skill of the hands rather than the plan.

The piping plover nests in open sand, where a fox can empty a clutch of eggs in seconds.
When a fox fixes on her nest, the hen flutters away from it, one wing dragging in the sand as though snapped — an irresistible, catchable meal.

Biologists describe the display as a ruse aimed at a single audience: it begins only when a predator is watching, leads it thirty or forty meters from the eggs, and ends the moment the distance is safe, the 'broken' wing folding neatly for takeoff.
The fox gets nothing; the deception was priced for exactly one buyer.
